other.text: Restoring the functional headline restored understanding — without losing any of the update's improvements. V2 keeps every V1 copy change except the slogan, and understanding came all the way back because the page says what it is again.

Concept 199 Avatar Chat Everpure is introducing a human avatar as its website chat guide, and we tested two name and voice candidates, Everly and Valencia, with about 170 people from the same B2B audience used in past rounds. The goal was to learn which persona people understand, trust, and want to talk to before committing to one for launch.
Concept 200 Sales Contact Form
We compared the live Contact Sales page against a proposed 2026 copy update to see which one helps visitors understand what the page is for and what happens next.
Here are the biggest findings from this round of testing:
YouTube content is strong, but the channel reads like marketing instead of a learning destination.

People found the content educational once they looked at it, but only 25% described the channel as an educational resource. Most visitors saw company programming before content organized around their problems, making the channel feel promotional rather than a trusted place to learn.
The VMware campaign is delivering qualified traffic, but the conversion experience is optimized for the wrong next step.

The ad successfully sets expectations, and people can easily find the Buyer's Guide. The bigger issue is that visitors consistently choose to watch a demo instead of filling out the guide form. They want to experience the product before they're willing to exchange their contact information.

Our focus should shift from messaging to experience. Across both studies, the positioning is largely working. The biggest opportunities are in content organization and conversion flow. For YouTube, we'll reorganize the channel around customer challenges and benchmark against leading competitors.
Here's the deck we'll review: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/16X0srJ1iGnO0Pl5hb8sA8ZK9rdcUcVU0tBJZsjX-r_8/edit?usp=sharing
Session Takeaways: We want to organize around what customers are trying to do, let them experience value before asking for commitment, and use simpler, more direct language throughout.

Rework the YouTube channel around customer problems. Shift the channel from company programming to an educational destination organized around key challenges, use cases, and playlists. The content itself is useful, but people still struggle to understand what Everpure does and where to start.

Update the virtualization campaign to a demo-first journey. Keep the ad-to-page messaging, but make the demo part of the conversion rather than a competing path. Test gating or bundling the demo with the Buyer's Guide, remove secondary distractions, and add proof to the benefit cards. Demo first-clicks were 43% versus 11% for the guide.

Get the next concepts into testing. Brandon needs to provide the hunch/angle for the chatbot experience so we can quickly build a test, while the team should also bring the video work into a campaign context rather than testing the video in isolation. This gives us a clearer way to measure whether each experience actually helps users move forward.
We'll focus on three key takeaways from our EDC Blueprint Assessment testing:
The assessment is easy to engage with. Positioning it as a short, personalized experience sets the right expectations.
3 Steps
2 Minutes
Personalized Results
The one-question-per-screen format significantly reduced perceived complexity.

The flow creates meaningful intent. Eight out of ten participants were ready to take the next step, split almost evenly between booking a workshop and downloading the blueprint. Only 16% indicated they would leave after completing it.

The opportunity now is integration. We'll discuss how this assessment becomes a stronger entry point from the EDC Blueprint pages and how to better connect it into the broader product journey. The assessment itself is validating well, so the next challenge is getting more qualified visitors into it.
Here are the findings
The new Contextual Intelligence page is a large improvement over the baseline.
Visitors want to watch before they commit.
The page is asking for high-commitment action before delivering the proof visitors need to justify it, and the demo video is the trust step that earns that conversion.
Watch Demo intent grew from 49% to 65%, and of the 47 visitors who clicked a CTA on the page, 41 (87%) chose Watch Demo or Watch Video.

Visitors understand the category but cannot articulate the positioning. The pages communicate through technical vocabulary that self-rates as understood but doesn't transfer, people leave knowing it's "data storage," not why it's different.

Here are the biggest takeaways from the work session:
The lighter, outcome-focused direction is moving the page in the right direction by reducing complexity and improving sentiment.
The biggest remaining opportunity is helping users understand what they'll receive from the assessment before asking them to start.

We should continue clarifying the relationship between the assessment, the Blueprint, and the workshop, while using the new "What's an EDC?" path to educate users without disrupting the primary journey.
The concept has a strong opportunity to connect with organizations still relying on legacy storage approaches.
Focus on communicating the business risks of the current approach before introducing the solution, then create a clear path into the assessment and contact experience.
The architecture is becoming easier to understand, but users still interpret it as a storage platform before recognizing the intelligence story.
Lead with the customer outcome first and use the diagram as supporting evidence rather than the primary message.
Continue simplifying terminology and reducing visual density, especially for first-time visitors.
The research continues to reinforce that users respond best when we clearly explain what they'll gain before asking them to take action. Looking forward to seeing the next round of iterations.

The team kept arriving at the same conclusion: be more direct. The designs become harder to understand when vision language, architecture, and multiple actions are layered together. Even the AI-generated Future of Storage concepts suffered when they lacked sufficient context about the business outcome on the other side of the page.
Make the journey explicit. The new iteration didn't create much lift. The infographic improved visually, but the page still has competing agendas between the Blueprint, Assessment, and Workshop.

Takeaway: Turn these into a clear linear story: understand EDC → see what the Blueprint provides → take the assessment → book the workshop. Make the assessment purpose and outcome much more explicit rather than relying on abstract language like "Map your path."

Don't make users decode the architecture Users clicked all over the diagram and didn't immediately understand what was interactive or what "Universal Data Intelligence" meant. Once content was revealed, comprehension was better, suggesting the information itself isn't necessarily the problem.

Takeaway: Make interactions obvious, show users what they'll get before they click, and consider offering high-level vs. technical paths. The infographic should probably support the platform story rather than be responsible for explaining it on its own.
Start with the customer's problem

The older page performed better than the new direction because its purpose and actions were more concrete. The new page starts with broad vision language like "Future of Enterprise Storage," followed by ambiguous actions such as "Take the Next Step" and "Explore AI Readiness."

Takeaway: Orient the page around the customer's current problem and then explain how Everpure helps solve it. Replace vague CTAs with explicit actions like Book a Demo, Take the Assessment, or "Here's how we get started." The page should make the progression from problem → value → solution → action obvious.

Make the assessment the clear primary journey. Position it as a quick, valuable 2-minute experience, explain what users get from it, and make the Blueprint and Workshop logical next steps rather than competing CTAs.

Simplify the EDC story. The page is asking users to process too much at once. Explain EDC in plain language, reduce the infographic to the few ideas users need now, and progressively reveal deeper technical detail.

Design for comprehension before sentiment. The page feels overwhelming and complicated, but the bigger opportunity is not simply changing colors. Improve hierarchy, vocabulary, and storytelling first, then explore how the heavy use of brown may be suppressing joy and excitement.
